Let’s talk about something that takes real bravery— the courage to choose change.
Change almost never feels comfortable, does it? Even when we know deep down that something isn’t working, the thought of doing things differently can feel overwhelming.
The therapist noticed this not just in her clients, but in herself, too—how easily people, all of us really, cling to what’s familiar, even when it hurts.
Take her client who was stuck in a job that just drained her spirit. She spent months talking about leaving, but just couldn’t quite take the leap. Why? She was worried—about letting her family down, about money, about what might happen next. In therapy, she finally started to say those fears out loud. And as she did, she began to picture what life might be like on the other side of change.
The day she finally handed in her resignation? She felt a wild mix of terror and exhilaration. It wasn’t easy—but it was her choice.
Then there was another client, caught in the same old cycle of unhealthy relationships. He knew the patterns—could list them off without missing a beat. Still, he kept getting pulled back in. In therapy, he realized: change isn’t just about having more willpower. It’s about understanding the deeper needs and fears that drive your decisions. With time, he learned to set boundaries, to say no, and most importantly, to trust that he actually deserved better.
And the therapist herself? She hit her own crossroads, questioning whether she wanted to keep practicing in the same way, or if she was really living in line with her own values. The process was messy—full of doubts, second-guessing, and a lot of soul-searching. But as she started to imagine new possibilities, hope slowly crept back in.
What becomes clear is that change isn’t always about huge, dramatic gestures. More often, it’s about those small, steady steps. It’s about showing up, even on the days you’re scared. It’s forgiving yourself when you stumble, and trying again.
Most of all, it’s about believing you’re worthy of something better.
Therapy became that safe space where change could actually happen—not because it was easy, but because it was supported.
In the end, the therapist and her clients learned something powerful— courage isn’t about having no fear. It’s about being willing to move forward, even when you’re afraid.
